metaData.originalTitle: How Snapchat Serves a Billion Predictions Per Second
metaData.title: How Snapchat Serves a Billion Predictions Per Second
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep-dive architectural analysis of Snap's Bento ML platform, detailing how it serves over a billion predictions per second by managing asymmetric ranking workloads, a split feature store, and a continuous feedback loop.
metaData.summary: The article explores the engineering behind Snapchat's Bento ML platform, which handles the immense scale of serving over a billion predictions per second for content ranking, ad auctions, friend suggestions, and AR lenses. It explains how the system is architected around the fundamental asymmetry of ranking requests, where a single user request expands into hundreds of candidate evaluations. The platform is split into a training half, which uses a layered code structure on Kubeflow for rapid experimentation, and a serving half, which tackles the hard operational problems of feature serving at scale. Key design choices include a split feature store (Robusta) to prevent train-serve skew, two strategies for handling high fanout (feature collocation and a dedicated Retrieval service), and a model export step that splits the compute graph between GPU and CPU. The article highlights a critical optimization where reducing serialization overhead led to a 2x latency reduction and 10x cost savings. A continuous feedback loop, with monitoring for drift and a Kubernetes-style reconciliation deployment system, ensures the platform can absorb massive growth, such as a 20x increase in model size over two years.

mainPoints.point: Ranking workloads are fundamentally asymmetric, driving the entire architecture.
mainPoints.explanation: A single user request expands into hundreds or thousands of (user, candidate) pairs that need scoring, creating a fan-out problem that shapes the design of retrieval, feature serving, and inference.

mainPoints.point: A split feature store is essential to prevent train-serve skew at scale.
mainPoints.explanation: Features must exist in both an offline analytical store (Apache Iceberg) for training and an online key-value store for serving. Snap's Robusta platform, built on Spark, keeps them in sync to prevent models from performing well in offline evaluation but poorly in production.

mainPoints.point: Optimizing the data plane, not just the model, yields the biggest performance gains.
mainPoints.explanation: Bento's engineers found that serialization and deserialization of feature data was a major latency bottleneck. By redesigning APIs to transfer features as raw bytes, they achieved a 2x latency reduction and 10x lower data plane costs.

keyQuotes: A ranking request is asymmetric. One user opens the app, and the platform has to decide what to show them out of millions of options.

The lesson is that at scale, the boring machinery of the system, including serialization, RPC framing, and network transport, often dominates the cost. Most of the cost lives outside the model itself.

The platform is less a fixed pipeline that produces a model and more a continuously running system that produces a stream of model versions, each one shaped by the data the previous version generated.

relatedArticles.title: The Architecture Behind Open-Source LLMs
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a comparative analysis of the architectural and training innovations driving frontier open-weight LLMs, focusing on MoE, attention mechanisms, and post-training strategies.

relatedArticles.title: How LinkedIn Feed Uses LLMs to Serve 1.3 Billion Users
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details LinkedIn's engineering journey to replace its complex, multi-system Feed retrieval architecture with a unified LLM-powered model, addressing challenges in data representation, training efficiency, sequential ranking, and massive-scale serving infrastructure.

relatedArticles.title: The Multi-Agent Trap
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article analyzes the 'Multi-Agent Trap' where unstructured AI architectures amplify errors, providing a research-backed playbook of proven patterns and failure prevention strategies for production-grade agentic systems.

relatedArticles.title: How OpenAI delivers low-latency voice AI at scale
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI rearchitected its WebRTC stack using a split relay and transceiver model to deliver low-latency voice AI at scale, solving port exhaustion and state stickiness in Kubernetes.

relatedArticles.title: Lessons from building Claude Code: Prompt caching is everything | Claude
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the critical, often unintuitive, lessons learned from optimizing prompt caching in Claude Code, emphasizing that designing an agent's entire architecture around prefix-matching caching is essential for performance and cost.

relatedArticles.title: A Guide to Context Engineering for LLMs
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A comprehensive guide to context engineering that explains why more context can degrade LLM performance and outlines four core strategies—Write, Select, Compress, and Isolate—to optimize model outputs.

relatedArticles.title: State of the Claw
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenClaw founder and OpenAI engineer Peter Steinberger discusses the unprecedented growth and security challenges of the OpenClaw project, shares his unique AI-assisted development workflow, and explores the evolving concept of 'engineer taste' in the AI era.

relatedArticles.title: How Spotify Ships to 675 Million Users Every Week Without Breaking Things
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores Spotify's release architecture, detailing how they ship weekly updates to 675 million users using trunk-based development, layered exposure rings, and automated state machines.

relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineer Ryan Lopopolo introduces 'Harness Engineering,' a paradigm shift where engineers design systems and automated guardrails to orchestrate hundreds of AI agents, transforming from coders to directors of software development.
